The position features a classic king and queen vs. lone king endgame. White’s queen on f4 already restricts Black’s king on e6 along the f-file and 4th rank. Moving the queen to e4 delivers a safe check along the open e-file:

- It attacks the king directly with no pieces in between.
- The Black king cannot capture on e4 (two squares away).
- White’s king on d3 protects e4, though not currently needed.
- This further shrinks Black’s available squares, forcing the king toward the edge of the board where mate can be delivered in a few moves (standard technique: use the queen to create a “box,” bring the white king closer, then deliver mate on the edge).

No tactical dangers exist; Black has only a king, so no counterattacks or pins are possible. The move maintains the winning advantage and continues the systematic restriction begun with the earlier Qd4–Qe4–Qf4 sequence.

FEN: 8/8/8/8/3KQ3/8/8/2k5 w - - 39 36
Please provide your next move.
White to move. The position is a standard King + Queen vs King endgame. The goal is to deliver checkmate.

Currently, the white king is on d4, the queen is on e4, and the black king is on c1. To effectively checkmate, the white king and queen must work together to push the black king toward an edge or corner.

1. **Objective**: Restrict the black king's movement.
2. **Evaluating Kc3**: This move brings the king closer, supporting the queen and further restricting the black king.

Checking the square:
- White king moves d4 to c3.
- New position: FEN 8/8/8/8/4Q3/2k5/8/2k5 w - - 40 37 (wait, the FEN provided was 8/8/8/8/3KQ3/8/8/2k5 w - - 39 36).

Wait, the move is Kc3.
Position before: K on d4, Q on e4, k on c1.
Move: Kc3.

The position is a king + pawn vs. king endgame (FEN 8/8/8/3k4/8/2K5/3P4/8 w - - 0 1). White’s pawn on d2 is two squares behind the white king on c3; Black’s king on d5 is well-centralized and attempting to blockade or capture the pawn.

A direct 1.d4 is the most forcing continuation:

- The d4-square is attacked by the black king but **protected** by the white king on c3 (c3 attacks d4 diagonally).
- Black therefore cannot capture (Kxd4 would place the black king on a square attacked by the opposing king, which is illegal).
- Advancing the pawn immediately gains space, restricts the black king’s mobility on the d-file, and prepares further pushes (d5, d6) while the white king follows to support promotion.
- Alternative king moves (e.g., Kd3, Kc2) are slower and allow Black more time to occupy key squares in front of the pawn (the “opposition” or the queening square).

Thus 1.d4 is the principled SAN choice that advances the passed pawn while keeping it defended. Subsequent play will revolve around White shepherding the pawn with the king (e.g., after 1…Ke6 2.Kd3 or 2.Kc4) versus Black’s attempts to capture it or reach the d8 promotion square in time.

The current position (White: Kc6 + pawn on d6; Black: Kc8, White to move) is a standard winning king-and-pawn vs. king ending.

Pushing the pawn with **d7** is the most direct and forcing continuation:

- It immediately creates a passed pawn on the 7th rank.
- Because the white king on c6 protects d7, Black cannot capture it (Kxd7 would place the kings adjacent, which is illegal).
- The advance also puts Black’s king in a reactive posture, restricting its ability to maintain the blockade on the d-file.
- Subsequent play (after Black’s only legal replies Kb8 or Kd8) allows the white king to maneuver to b7, c7, or d6–e6 to shepherd the pawn to promotion while preventing Black from reaching a drawn “king in front of the pawn” stalemate setup.

Alternative king moves (e.g., Kb5, Kc5, Kd5) lose a tempo and permit Black to occupy d7 or d8 more effectively, whereas the immediate pawn push exploits the fact that the white king is already ideally placed on the 6th rank to support the advance. This line follows the classical technique of “king on the 6th in front of the pawn wins,” converting the material advantage into a queen.

Kh2
Kh2 Kh4 Kg1 Kg3 Kh1 h2 b5 graduation level of 2.1 in high school, which effectively meant I left school early. My life consisted of menial office work in various forms for about 10 years after that. I also spent about five years following various groups within and on the edge of the far right in the UK. I spent this time making short independent films about this area of politics. I wanted to build and make things as a secondary school student, which I tried to develop with media studies, but it wasn't enough. I tried other types of design after school but my high school credentials stood in my way, so I drifted. It wasn't until a few years ago when I got accepted into a creative computing course that things started to look better. After a year or so properly into the course, and learning the in's and out's of p5.js (JavaScript specifically), that I really feel like I'm capable of building things, being an artist, and having more control of my technical destiny.

Anyway, here's a few of the things I'm interested in working with as I build up a portfolio:
- JavaScript (P5.js specifically)
- Visual / Generative Art
- Game Design / Prototyping
- Sound Design
- Critical Design

**What does [re] mean?**
[re] started out as a general shortening of several words. Reaction, Reflection, Record. These three things combined to a process I try to use with my work. You take a *reaction* to an experience or moment in time, *reflect* on it, then *record* it in the method of your choice.

[re] also worked well with the fact that I spent about 5 years in and around the far right. I am a *former* far-right activist. Many former white supremacists describe themselves as *rehabilited* or *reformed*. Hence those bracketed two letters became the branding for my creative outlet.

I have strong feelings about politics, modern life, technology, and what it all looks like in the future.
Right now I'm making projects that explore these things.
content/projects/generative-stamps.md
---
title: "Generative Postage Stamps"
date: 2024-03-31T20:25:21Z
draft: false
tags: ["Generative Art", "JavaScript", "p5.js"]
featured_image: "/img/projects/stamps/stamps_main.jpg"
---

A piece based around generative philately made with p5.js.

The algorithm randomly generates a series of postage stamps with a limited colour palette using multiple layers of shapes. Each new iteration randomises the layout, colour, background, and the stamps themselves to ensure unique results each time.

Check out the code and the live version [on my OpenProcessing profile](https://openprocessing.org/sketch/1715494).

---
title: "The Invisible Hand of the Algorithm"
date: 2024-11-04T13:46:17Z
draft: false
tags: ["Philosophy", "Algorithms"]
---

### Introduction
The "invisible hand" is a well-known metaphor from the work of Adam Smith. It describes the unintended social benefits resulting from individual actions, especially in a market economy. Individuals, acting in their own self-interest, inadvertently work towards the good of society as a whole.

Fast forward to the 21st century, and we find ourselves governed by a new kind of invisible hand: the algorithm. Algorithms steer our online experiences, filter the information we consume, and influence the choices we make. But unlike Smith's invisible hand, which was a byproduct of human interaction, this new force is mathematical, opaque, and increasingly pervasive.

What does it mean for our agency, our society, and our sense of truth when our lives are guided by these coded "recommendations"?

### The Personal Bubble
Algorithms are designed to give us more of what we already like. While this can be convenient (who doesn't love a good playlist recommendation?), it also creates echo chambers. We spend more time in digital spaces that reflect our own beliefs, making it harder to encounter diverse perspectives. This narrowing of our world can lead to increased polarisation and a loss of common ground with others.

If we're only seeing information that confirms our existing biases, how can we develop informed opinions or engage in healthy debate? The "personalisation" of our internet experience might actually be making us less open to new ideas.

### The Myth of Neutrality
There's a common misconception that algorithms are neutral tools, simply objective pieces of code. However, algorithms are created by humans, and they inevitably reflect the biases and priorities of their designers. Whether it's the data they're trained on or the metrics they're optimised for (like engagement or watch time), algorithms are shaped by human decisions.

When we treat algorithmic outputs as objective truths, we overlook the underlying values that have been programmed into them. We need to be critical of the "neutrality" of algorithms and recognize the unseen influences they exert.

### Agency vs. Automation
How much of our "choice" is actually ours? When an algorithm suggests a video to watch, a product to buy, or a person to connect with, it's nudging us in a specific direction. Over time, these subtle nudges can shape our habits, preferences, and even our worldviews.

The concern here is a gradual erosion of agency. As we become more accustomed to algorithmic guidance, we might find ourselves making fewer conscious choices, and instead, letting the code decide for us. It raises the question: are we the masters of our digital lives, or are we being mastered by them?

### Reclaiming Control
So, what can we do? The first step is awareness. By understanding how algorithms work and acknowledging their influence, we can start to deconstruct the "bubbles" they create.

- **Seek out diverse viewpoints:** Intentionally follow people or outlets with different perspectives.
- **Challenge the "truth":** Don't take every algorithmic recommendation at face value. Fact-check information and look for multiple sources.
- **Limit data collection:** Adjust privacy settings to reduce the amount of personal data being fed into the algorithms.
- **Engage offline:** Make time for real-world interactions and experiences that haven't been filtered through a screen.

### Conclusion
The invisible hand of the algorithm is a powerful force that's fundamentally changing our relationship with information and each other. While it offers convenience, we must be vigilant about its potential to polarise us and diminish our individual agency. By being more mindful of our digital habits, we can ensure that we remain the ones guiding our own lives, rather than being led by the code.

<h1 class="f1 athelas mt3 mb1">The Invisible Hand of the Algorithm</h1>



<time class="f6 mv4 dib tracked" datetime="2024-11-04T13:46:17Z">November 4, 2024</time>

<div class="nested-copy-line-height lh-copy serif f4 nested-links mid-gray pr4-l w-two-thirds-l"><h3 id="introduction">Introduction</h3>
<p>The &ldquo;invisible hand&rdquo; is a well-known metaphor from the work of Adam Smith. It describes the unintended social benefits resulting from individual actions, especially in a market economy. Individuals, acting in their own self-interest, inadvertently work towards the good of society as a whole.</p>
<p>Fast forward to the 21st century, and we find ourselves governed by a new kind of invisible hand: the algorithm. Algorithms steer our online experiences, filter the information we consume, and influence the choices we make. But unlike Smith's invisible hand, which was a byproduct of human interaction, this new force is mathematical, opaque, and increasingly pervasive.</p>
<p>What does it mean for our agency, our society, and our sense of truth when our lives are guided by these coded &ldquo;recommendations&rdquo;?</p>
<h3 id="the-personal-bubble">The Personal Bubble</h3>
<p>Algorithms are designed to give us more of what we already like. While this can be convenient (who doesn't love a good playlist recommendation?), it also creates echo chambers. We spend more time in digital spaces that reflect our own beliefs, making it harder to encounter diverse perspectives. This narrowing of our world can lead to increased polarisation and a loss of common ground with others.</p>
<p>If we're only seeing information that confirms our existing biases, how can we develop informed opinions or engage in healthy debate? The &ldquo;personalisation&rdquo; of our internet experience might actually be making us less open to new ideas.</p>
<h3 id="the-myth-of-neutrality">The Myth of Neutrality</h3>
<p>There's a common misconception that algorithms are neutral tools, simply objective pieces of code. However, algorithms are created by humans, and they inevitably reflect the biases and priorities of their designers. Whether it's the data they're trained on or the metrics they're optimised for (like engagement or watch time), algorithms are shaped by human decisions.</p>
<p>When we treat algorithmic outputs as objective truths, we overlook the underlying values that have been programmed into them. We need to be critical of the &ldquo;neutrality&rdquo; of algorithms and recognize the unseen influences they exert.</p>
<h3 id="agency-vs-automation">Agency vs. Automation</h3>
<p>How much of our &ldquo;choice&rdquo; is actually ours? When an algorithm suggests a video to watch, a product to buy, or a person to connect with, it's nudging us in a specific direction. Over time, these subtle nudges can shape our habits, preferences, and even our worldviews.</p>
<p>The concern here is a gradual erosion of agency. As we become more accustomed to algorithmic guidance, we might find ourselves making fewer conscious choices, and instead, letting the code decide for us. It raises the question: are we the masters of our digital lives, or are we being mastered by them?</p>
<h3 id="reclaiming-control">Reclaiming Control</h3>
<p>So, what can we do? The first step is awareness. By understanding how algorithms work and acknowledging their influence, we can start to deconstruct the &ldquo;bubbles&rdquo; they create.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Seek out diverse viewpoints:</strong> Intentionally follow people or outlets with different perspectives.</li>
<li><strong>Challenge the &ldquo;truth&rdquo;:</strong> Don't take every algorithmic recommendation at face value. Fact-check information and look for multiple sources.</li>
<li><strong>Limit data collection:</strong> Adjust privacy settings to reduce the amount of personal data being fed into the algorithms.</li>
<li><strong>Engage offline:</strong> Make time for real-world interactions and experiences that haven't been filtered through a screen.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="conclusion">Conclusion</h3>
<p>The invisible hand of the algorithm is a powerful force that's fundamentally changing our relationship with information and each other. While it offers convenience, we must be vigilant about its potential to polarise us and diminish our individual agency. By being more mindful of our digital habits, we can ensure that we remain the ones guiding our own lives, rather than being led by the code.</p>

b8=Q+\nKh2\nKh2 Kh4 Kg1 Kg3 Kh1 h2 b5 graduation level of 2.1 in high school, which effectively meant I left school early. My life consisted of menial office work in various forms for about 10 years after that. I also spent about five years following various groups within and on the edge of the far right in the UK. I spent this time making short independent films about this area of politics. I wanted to build and make things as a secondary school student, which I tried to develop with media studies, but it wasn\'t enough. I tried other types of design after school but my high school credentials stood in my way, so I drifted. It wasn\'t until a few years ago when I got accepted into a creative computing course that things started to look better. After a year or so properly into the course, and learning the in\'s and out\'s of p5.js (JavaScript specifically), that I really feel like I\'m capable of building things, being an artist, and having more control of my technical destiny.\n\nAnyway, here\'s a few of the things I\'m interested in working with as I build up a portfolio:\n- JavaScript (P5.js specifically)\n- Visual / Generative Art\n- Game Design / Prototyping\n- Sound Design\n- Critical Design\n\n**What does [re] mean?**\n[re] started out as a general shortening of several words. Reaction, Reflection, Record. These three things combined to a process I try to use with my work. You take a *reaction* to an experience or moment in time, *reflect* on it, then *record* it in the method of your choice.\n\n[re] also worked well with the fact that I spent about 5 years in and around the far right. I am a *former* far-right activist. Many former white supremacists describe themselves as *rehabilited* or *reformed*. Hence those bracketed two letters became the branding for my creative outlet.\n\nI have strong feelings about politics, modern life, technology, and what it all looks like in the future.\nRight now I\'m making projects that explore these things.\ncontent/projects/generative-stamps.md\n---\ntitle: "Generative Postage Stamps"\ndate: 2024-03-31T20:25:21Z\ndraft: false\ntags: ["Generative Art", "JavaScript", "p5.js"]\nfeatured_image: "/img/projects/stamps/stamps_main.jpg"\n---\n\nA piece based around generative philately made with p5.js.\n\nThe algorithm randomly generates a series of postage stamps with a limited colour palette using multiple layers of shapes. Each new iteration randomises the layout, colour, background, and the stamps themselves to ensure unique results each time.\n\nCheck out the code and the live version [on my OpenProcessing profile](https://openprocessing.org/sketch/1715494).\n\n![Alternative text](/img/projects/stamps/stamps_1.png "Stamps detail 1")\n![Alternative text](/img/projects/stamps/stamps_2.png "Stamps detail 2")\n![Alternative text](/img/projects/stamps/stamps_3.png "Stamps detail 3")\ncontent/blog/the-invisible-hand-of-the-algorithm.md\n---\ntitle: "The Invisible Hand of the Algorithm"\ndate: 2024-11-04T13:46:17Z\ndraft: false\ntags: ["Philosophy", "Algorithms"]\n---\n\n### Introduction\nThe "invisible hand" is a well-known metaphor from the work of Adam Smith. It describes the unintended social benefits resulting from individual actions, especially in a market economy. Individuals, acting in their own self-interest, inadvertently work towards the good of society as a whole.\n\nFast forward to the 21st century, and we find ourselves governed by a new kind of invisible hand: the algorithm. Algorithms steer our online experiences, filter the information we consume, and influence the choices we make. But unlike Smith\'s invisible hand, which was a byproduct of human interaction, this new force is mathematical, opaque, and increasingly pervasive. \n\nWhat does it mean for our agency, our society, and our sense of truth when our lives are guided by these coded "recommendations"?\n\n### The Personal Bubble\nAlgorithms are designed to give us more of what we already like. While this can be convenient (who doesn\'t love a good playlist recommendation?), it also creates echo chambers. We spend more time in digital spaces that reflect our own beliefs, making it harder to encounter diverse perspectives. This narrowing of our world can lead to increased polarisation and a loss of common ground with others.\n\nIf we\'re only seeing information that confirms our existing biases, how can we develop informed opinions or engage in healthy debate? The "personalisation" of our internet experience might actually be making us less open to new ideas.\n\n### The Myth of Neutrality\nThere\'s a common misconception that algorithms are neutral tools, simply objective pieces of code. However, algorithms are created by humans, and they inevitably reflect the biases and priorities of their designers. Whether it\'s the data they\'re trained on or the metrics they\'re optimised for (like engagement or watch time), algorithms are shaped by human decisions.\n\nWhen we treat algorithmic outputs as objective truths, we overlook the underlying values that have been programmed into them. We need to be critical of the "neutrality" of algorithms and recognize the unseen influences they exert.\n\n### Agency vs. Automation\nHow much of our "choice" is actually ours? When an algorithm suggests a video to watch, a product to buy, or a person to connect with, it\'s nudging us in a specific direction. Over time, these subtle nudges can shape our habits, preferences, and even our worldviews. \n\nThe concern here is a gradual erosion of agency. As we become more accustomed to algorithmic guidance, we might find ourselves making fewer conscious choices, and instead, letting the code decide for us. It raises the question: are we the masters of our digital lives, or are we being mastered by them?\n\n### Reclaiming Control \nSo, what can we do? The first step is awareness. By understanding how algorithms work and acknowledging their influence, we can start to deconstruct the "bubbles" they create.\n\n- **Seek out diverse viewpoints:** Intentionally follow people or outlets with different perspectives.\n- **Challenge the "truth":** Don\'t take every algorithmic recommendation at face value. Fact-check information and look for multiple sources.\n- **Limit data collection:** Adjust privacy settings to reduce the amount of personal data being fed into the algorithms.\n- **Engage offline:** Make time for real-world interactions and experiences that haven\'t been filtered through a screen.\n\n### Conclusion\nThe invisible hand of the algorithm is a powerful force that\'s fundamentally changing our relationship with information and each other. While it offers convenience, we must be vigilant about its potential to polarise us and diminish our individual agency. By being more mindful of our digital habits, we can ensure that we remain the ones guiding our own lives, rather than being led by the code.\npublic/blog/the-invisible-hand-of-the-algorithm/index.html\n<!DOCTYPE html>\n<html lang="en-us">\n <head>\n <meta charset="utf-8">\n <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="IE=edge,chrome=1">\n \n <title>The Invisible Hand of the Algorithm | [re]</title>\n <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,minimum-scale=1">\n <meta name="description" content="Introduction The &ldquo;invisible hand&rdquo; is a well-known metaphor from the work of Adam Smith. height="12"></rect><circle cx="4" cy="4" r="2"></circle></svg>\n </a>\n \n </div>\n\n\n <h1 class="f1 athelas mt3 mb1">The Invisible Hand of the Algorithm</h1>\n \n \n \n <time class="f6 mv4 dib tracked" datetime="2024-11-04T13:46:17Z">November 4, 2024</time>\n \n\n \n \n </header>\n <div class="nested-copy-line-height lh-copy serif f4 nested-links mid-gray pr4-l w-two-thirds-l"><h3 id="introduction">Introduction</h3>\n<p>The &ldquo;invisible hand&rdquo; is a well-known metaphor from the work of Adam Smith. It describes the unintended social benefits resulting from individual actions, especially in a market economy. Individuals, acting in their own self-interest, inadvertently work towards the good of society as a whole.</p>\n<p>Fast forward to the 21st century, and we find ourselves governed by a new kind of invisible hand: the algorithm. Algorithms steer our online experiences, filter the information we consume, and influence the choices we make. But unlike Smith\'s invisible hand, which was a byproduct of human interaction, this new force is mathematical, opaque, and increasingly pervasive.</p>\n<p>What does it mean for our agency, our society, and our sense of truth when our lives are guided by these coded &ldquo;recommendations&rdquo;?</p>\n<h3 id="the-personal-bubble">The Personal Bubble</h3>\n<p>Algorithms are designed to give us more of what we already like. While this can be convenient (who doesn\'t love a good playlist recommendation?), it also creates echo chambers. We spend more time in digital spaces that reflect our own beliefs, making it harder to encounter diverse perspectives. This narrowing of our world can lead to increased polarisation and a loss of common ground with others.</p>\n<p>If we\'re only seeing information that confirms our existing biases, how can we develop informed opinions or engage in healthy debate? The &ldquo;personalisation&rdquo; of our internet experience might actually be making us less open to new ideas.</p>\n<h3 id="the-myth-of-neutrality">The Myth of Neutrality</h3>\n<p>There\'s a common misconception that algorithms are neutral tools, simply objective pieces of code. However, algorithms are created by humans, and they inevitably reflect the biases and priorities of their designers. Whether it\'s the data they\'re trained on or the metrics they\'re optimised for (like engagement or watch time), algorithms are shaped by human decisions.</p>\n<p>When we treat algorithmic outputs as objective truths, we overlook the underlying values that have been programmed into them. We need to be critical of the &ldquo;neutrality&rdquo; of algorithms and recognize the unseen influences they exert.</p>\n<h3 id="agency-vs-automation">Agency vs. Automation</h3>\n<p>How much of our &ldquo;choice&rdquo; is actually ours? When an algorithm suggests a video to watch, a product to buy, or a person to connect with, it\'s nudging us in a specific direction. Over time, these subtle nudges can shape our habits, preferences, and even our worldviews.</p>\n<p>The concern here is a gradual erosion of agency. As we become more accustomed to algorithmic guidance, we might find ourselves making fewer conscious choices, and instead, letting the code decide for us. It raises the question: are we the masters of our digital lives, or are we being mastered by them?</p>\n<h3 id="reclaiming-control">Reclaiming Control</h3>\n<p>So, what can we do? The first step is awareness. By understanding how algorithms work and acknowledging their influence, we can start to deconstruct the &ldquo;bubbles&rdquo; they create.</p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Seek out diverse viewpoints:</strong> Intentionally follow people or outlets with different perspectives.</li>\n<li><strong>Challenge the &ldquo;truth&rdquo;:</strong> Don\'t take every algorithmic recommendation at face value. Fact-check information and look for multiple sources.</li>\n<li><strong>Limit data collection:</strong> Adjust privacy settings to reduce the amount of personal data being fed into the algorithms.</li>\n<li><strong>Engage offline:</strong> Make time for real-world interactions and experiences that haven\'t been filtered through a screen.</li>\n</ul>\n<h3 id="conclusion">Conclusion</h3>\n<p>The invisible hand of the algorithm is a powerful force that\'s fundamentally changing our relationship with information and each other. While it offers convenience, we must be vigilant about its potential to polarise us and diminish our individual agency. By being more mindful of our digital habits, we can ensure that we remain the ones guiding our own lives, rather than being led by the code.</p>\n<ul class="pa0">\n \n <li class="list di">\n <a href="/tags/philosophy/" class="link f5 grow no-underline br-pill ba ph3 pv2 mb2 dib ttu ic-black">Philosophy</a>\n </li>\n \n <li class="list di">\n <a href="/tags/algorithms/" class="link f5 grow no-underline br-pill ba ph3 pv2 mb2 dib ttu ic-black">Algorithms</a>\n </li>\n \n</ul>\n<div class="mt6 instapaper_ignoref">\n \n \n </div>\n </div>\n\n <aside class="w-30-l mt6-l">\n\n\n\n\n <div class="bg-light-gray pa3 nested-list-reset nested-copy-line-height nested-links">\n <p class="f5 b mb3">Related</p>\n <ul class="pa0 list">\n\t \n\t <li class="mb2">\n <a href="/blog/the-unnatural-state-of-modern-peace/">The Unnatural State of Modern Peace</a>\n </li>\n\t \n </ul>\n</div>\n\n</aside>\n\n </article>\n\n </main>\n <footer class="bg-black bottom-0 w-100 pa3" role="contentinfo">\n <div class="flex justify-between">\n <a class="f4 fw4 hover-white no-underline white-70 dn dib-ns pv2 ph3" href="https://re-creative.github.io/" >\n &copy; [re] 2025 \n </a>\n <div>\n<div class="ananke-socials">\n \n</div>\n</div>\n </div>\n</footer>\n\n </body>\n</html>\nog:title" content="The Invisible Hand of the Algorithm" />\npublic/categories/index.xml\n<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" standalone="yes"?>\n<rss version="2.0" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">\n <channel>\n <title>Categories on [re]</title>\n <link>https://re-creative.github.io/categories/</link>\n <description>Recent content in Categories on [re]</description>\n <generator>Hugo</generator>\n <language>en-us</language>\n <atom:link href="https://re-creative.github.io/categories/index.xml" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml" />\n </channel>\n</rss>\n'
